title: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
summary: Timeline first in Nsight Systems, then per-kernel counters in Nsight Compute: read the Speed Of Light rows, compute occupancy and the SOL gap, and rank optimization candidates by the time they can actually return.
outcomes: Explain why a timeline pass in Nsight Systems comes before any per-kernel counter collection
Classify a kernel as memory bound, compute bound or latency bound from its Speed Of Light rows
Compute occupancy from block size, registers per thread and shared memory, and say which resource limits it
Compute the SOL gap of each kernel and rank candidates by gap times time share, including when to skip a large gap
Explain how clock locking, cache flushing, replay and serialization change the numbers the profiler reports

lessons.title: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes

blocks.md:
You have a CUDA application that runs one inference step in 14.52 ms and you want it faster. The longest kernel in the step is a 4096x4096 FP32 GEMM that takes 2.50 ms, and it is already running at 82 percent of the peak FP32 rate of the GPU. Spending a week on it can return at most a few percent of the step.

The roofline model, from the prerequisite course, already tells you the ceiling for one kernel: its time cannot go below the larger of its work divided by peak compute and its traffic divided by peak bandwidth. Profiling adds the two things roofline cannot give you: the measured position of a real kernel under that ceiling, and the time that is not inside any kernel at all.

NVIDIA ships two separate tools for these two questions, and the Nsight Compute triage guide is explicit about the order: use Nsight Systems first if kernel priority is unclear, then use Nsight Compute.

- **Nsight Systems** traces the whole process on a timeline: CPU threads, CUDA API calls, kernels, memory copies, synchronization. It answers *which* GPU work matters and how much time is not GPU work.
- **Nsight Compute** profiles one kernel launch at a time with hardware counters. It answers *why* a chosen kernel is as slow as it is.

Doing it the other way round is the classic beginner mistake: you collect beautiful counters for a kernel that holds 4 percent of the wall time.

nodes.label:
rank GPU work
by time share

scenes.caption: Level one. Trace the whole process and look at the timeline before you look at any counter.
Two outputs. Everything that is not GPU work (left column of the timeline) is fixed at this level, not with counters. What is left gets ranked by time share.
Level two. Only the kernels at the top of that ranking are worth a counter run, one kernel at a time.
Then close the loop: make one change, re-measure the kernel duration, and re-run the timeline because the bottleneck often moves somewhere else.

blocks.md:
What the Nsight Systems timeline shows, per the user guide: a CUDA API row inside each CPU thread holding the `cuda*` and `cu*` calls that thread made, and, near the bottom, a GPU node containing each CUDA context and its streams. Kernel launches are drawn in blue and memory transfers in red. Ranges from the NVIDIA Tools Extension (NVTX) that you add in your own code are drawn on the CPU threads and projected onto the GPU rows, which is how you label a phase like "attention" or "optimizer step".

The figure below is one iteration of our example application on an H100 SXM5. Three lanes: the CPU thread that drives the GPU, the copy engine, and the SMs.

scenes.caption: The traced iteration: 14.52 ms of wall time. Host prep, a blocking cudaMemcpy, seven kernels back to back, a copy back, host post-processing.
Now mark the SM lane where it is empty: 4.50 ms before the first kernel and 4.10 ms after the last one. The SMs run kernels for 5.92 of 14.52 ms, which is 40.8 percent of the iteration.
The copies are the other exposed cost: 3.50 ms of transfer that nothing overlaps, and the host sits blocked inside cudaMemcpy for all 2.40 ms of the upload.

Fixed at the timeline level: pinned buffers, cudaMemcpyAsync on a copy stream, host work for the next batch started early. The iteration is now 6.02 ms, a 2.41x speedup, and not one line of kernel code changed.

blocks.tex: U_{\text{GPU}} = \frac{\text{time with any GPU operation}}{\text{wall time}} \qquad U_{\text{SM}} = \frac{\text{time running kernels}}{\text{wall time}}
blocks.caption: Two different utilizations. The first counts copies as GPU work, the second does not.

blocks.md:
For this iteration: GPU busy time is 2.40 + 5.92 + 1.10 = 9.42 ms, so $U_{\text{GPU}} = 9.42/14.52 = 0.649$ and $U_{\text{SM}} = 5.92/14.52 = 0.408$. The gaps where the GPU does nothing at all total 5.10 ms, and the exposed copies another 3.50 ms.

So before you open a single counter you already know the budget: 8.60 of 14.52 ms, 59 percent of the iteration, is not kernel execution.

blocks.prompt: You get to do exactly one of these: (a) make both GEMMs twice as fast, or (b) pin the host buffers, make the copies async, and overlap host work with the GPU. Which one saves more wall time, and by how much?
blocks.reveal:
**(b), by a lot.**

(a) The two GEMMs are 5.00 ms of the 14.52 ms iteration. Halving them saves 2.50 ms: 14.52 goes to 12.02 ms, a 1.21x speedup. And 2x on a kernel already at 82 percent of peak FP32 is not physically available anyway.

(b) With the copies overlapped and the host off the critical path, the iteration becomes about max(host 5.00, kernels 5.92, copies 3.50) + 0.10 launch latency = 6.02 ms, a 2.41x speedup. Same kernels, same code inside them.

blocks.md: The GPU utilization that Nsight Systems reports is **time** utilization, not resource utilization. Its own guide says so: a single running memcpy counts as the same amount of utilization as a huge kernel that takes over all the cores, and concurrent operations in the same chunk can add up to more than 100 percent. A 100 percent busy GPU can still be doing almost nothing useful.

Nsight Systems can also find the standard timeline mistakes for you. `nsys analyze` runs expert-system rules over the exported SQLite database; the shipped rules are:

- **GPU Starvation**: GPU idle for longer than 500 ms (threshold adjustable). It deliberately excludes the gap before the first and after the last GPU operation, and profiling overhead inside a gap.
- **GPU Low Utilization**: splits the active range into chunks and reports the ones below a threshold.
- **Synchronous Memcpy** and **Synchronous Memset**: transfers that block the host; the advice is the `*Async` variants.
- **Asynchronous memcpy with pageable memory**: an async copy that silently becomes synchronous because the memory was not pinned. This is exactly our 2.40 ms upload.
- **Synchronization APIs**: calls that block the host until all issued CUDA work completes.

blocks.code:
# level one: trace the process, then summarize and run the rules
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o step --force-overwrite true ./app

# where does GPU time go? (these two are in the default stats set)
nsys stats --report cuda_gpu_kern_sum --report cuda_gpu_mem_time_sum step.nsys-rep

# launch call vs queue wait vs kernel execution, per launch
nsys stats --report cuda_kern_exec_trace step.nsys-rep

# the shipped expert rules
nsys analyze --rule gpu_gaps,gpu_time_util,cuda_memcpy_sync,cuda_memcpy_async,cuda_api_sync step.nsys-rep
blocks.caption: Nsight Systems CLI. cuda_gpu_kern_sum gives the per-kernel time share that drives the whole ranking in lesson 4.

blocks.md: One subtlety from the `cuda_kern_exec_trace` documentation that catches people out. The report splits each launch into API time on the CPU, queue time between the launch call and the start of execution, and kernel time on the GPU. Queue time looks like waste, but the guide warns that it is not: queue time means the GPU was busy with other work when the kernel was scheduled. If every launch starts immediately with no queue time, that may indicate an idle GPU with poor utilization. Eliminating queue time is not a goal.
Remember the order. The timeline sets the denominator for everything else: a kernel that is 4 percent of the wall time can never give you more than 4 percent, however bad its counters look.

blocks.question: The timeline of our iteration shows 5.10 ms of total GPU idle. Which part of it will the GPU Starvation rule report by default?
options: All 5.10 ms, split into the three gaps it found
Only the 0.10 ms launch gap, because the other two are at the edges of the iteration
None of it: the rule's default threshold is 500 ms of continuous idle, and the largest gap here is 3.00 ms
The 4.10 ms gap only, because trailing gaps are the ones the host can fix
blocks.explain: The rule identifies time ranges where a GPU is idle for longer than 500 ms (adjustable). Millisecond-scale gaps inside a single iteration are far below that, so the rule stays silent and you still have to read the timeline yourself. GPU Low Utilization, which works on chunk percentages, is the rule that catches this shape of problem.

blocks.question: A colleague reports: "Nsight Systems says the GPU is 97 percent utilized, so the GPU is the bottleneck and we need better kernels." What is the hole in that reasoning?
options: Nothing: 97 percent time utilization means the SMs are 97 percent busy
Utilization there is time based, so a long exposed memcpy or a tiny kernel occupying one SM counts as full utilization
Nsight Systems cannot measure GPU utilization at all, only CPU time
It is wrong only if the application uses more than one CUDA stream
blocks.explain: The rule's own notes say the utilization is time utilization, not resource utilization: a single running memcpy counts the same as a huge kernel, and concurrent operations can sum past 100 percent. 97 percent busy could be 97 percent copying, or one kernel with a 1-block grid. Per-kernel counters, not timeline utilization, tell you whether the hardware is actually being used.

lessons.title: Reading the Speed Of Light rows

blocks.md:
Now level two. `ncu` collects hardware counters for one kernel launch and groups them into **sections**. Without options it collects the `basic` set; `--set full` collects everything, `--section <id>` picks one, `--metrics <name>` picks individual metrics.

The first section you read is **GPU Speed Of Light Throughput** (section id `SpeedOfLight`). Its own description: a high-level overview of the throughput for compute and memory resources of the GPU, where for each unit the throughput reports the achieved percentage of utilization with respect to the theoretical maximum, with breakdowns showing the throughput of each individual sub-metric so you can identify the highest contributor.

Two numbers carry the section:

- **Compute (SM) Throughput**, from `sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed`
- **Memory Throughput**, from `gpu__compute_memory_throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed`

Both are percentages of a peak sustained rate, averaged over unit instances. `elapsed` normalizes by all cycles in the kernel; the `active` variant normalizes only by cycles when the unit was doing something, so `active` is never lower than `elapsed`.

The critical detail about how they are built, from the metrics guide: **a throughput metric returns the maximum percentage value of its constituent counters.** Memory Throughput is a max over the L1, L2 and DRAM subsystems, not a sum and not an average. That is why the section ships with a breakdown, and why a single number can never be your diagnosis.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{SOL}_{\text{mem}} = \frac{\text{achieved bytes per second}}{\text{peak bytes per second}} \qquad \mathrm{SOL}_{\text{comp}} = \frac{\text{achieved FLOP per second}}{\text{peak FLOP per second}}
blocks.caption: What a percent-of-peak row means, for the DRAM constituent and for FP32 math. Nsight computes these from counters; below we reconstruct them by hand so the row stops being magic.

blocks.md:
Take the four distinct kernels from the iteration, all on 4096x4096 FP32 tensors, on an H100 SXM5 (peak HBM3 bandwidth 3,350 GB/s, peak FP32 67 TFLOP/s). For each one we know the work and the DRAM traffic analytically, so we can compute the two ratios from the measured duration alone.

- `sgemm_4096`: $2 \cdot 4096^3 = 137.44$ GFLOP, 3 matrices of 4 bytes = 201.33 MB
- `layernorm_fwd`: read and write the tensor = 134.22 MB, about 10 FLOP per element
- `softmax_rows`: two read passes and one write = 201.33 MB, about 6 FLOP per element
- `bias_add_relu`: read and write = 134.22 MB, 2 FLOP per element

blocks.code:
PEAK_BW, PEAK_FP32 = 3350e9, 67e12          # H100 SXM5
N = 4096; elems = N * N

# name, FLOP, DRAM bytes, measured duration (s)
k = [('sgemm_4096',    2*N**3,   3*elems*4, 2498.89e-6),
     ('layernorm_fwd', 10*elems, 2*elems*4,   51.62e-6),
     ('softmax_rows',  6*elems,  3*elems*4,  183.02e-6),
     ('bias_add_relu', 2*elems,  2*elems*4,  319.57e-6)]

for name, flop, byt, t in k:
    print(f'{name:14s} {byt/t/1e9:7.1f} GB/s = {byt/t/PEAK_BW*100:5.2f}% of DRAM peak | '
          f'{flop/t/1e12:6.2f} TFLOP/s = {flop/t/PEAK_FP32*100:5.2f}% of FP32 peak')

# sgemm_4096      80.6 GB/s =  2.40% of DRAM peak |  55.00 TFLOP/s = 82.09% of FP32 peak
# layernorm_fwd 2600.1 GB/s = 77.62% of DRAM peak |   3.25 TFLOP/s =  4.85% of FP32 peak
# softmax_rows  1100.0 GB/s = 32.84% of DRAM peak |   0.55 TFLOP/s =  0.82% of FP32 peak
# bias_add_relu  420.0 GB/s = 12.54% of DRAM peak |   0.10 TFLOP/s =  0.16% of FP32 peak
blocks.caption: Achieved rate divided by peak rate. These are the same ratios the Speed Of Light section reports, reconstructed from bytes, FLOP and duration.

scenes.caption: Compute: achieved FP32 rate as a percent of 67 TFLOP/s. Only the GEMM is anywhere near the math pipes.
DRAM: achieved bytes per second as a percent of 3,350 GB/s. The ordering inverts, and layernorm is close to the bus limit.
The limiter of each kernel is the larger of its two rows. Two kernels are near a ceiling, two are nowhere near anything.

blocks.prompt: bias_add_relu reports 12.5 percent memory and 0.16 percent compute, and its achieved occupancy is a healthy 75 percent. Is it memory bound, compute bound, or something else? What would you change first?
blocks.reveal:
**Neither: it is latency bound.** Both throughput rows are low, so no unit is near its ceiling; the warps are resident but not getting work issued or are waiting on memory.

The Nsight Compute triage guide routes exactly this case: both low means go to "what prevents instructions from issuing?", and high occupancy with low pipeline utilization means warps are present but not issuing. Adding more warps will not help. What helps is more work in flight per warp: unroll so each thread handles several elements, use vectorized 16-byte loads, issue loads early and consume them late. Raising occupancy is only the other half of the same lever.

blocks.md:
The triage guide gives the classification rule with explicit thresholds: below about 60 percent is low (latency-risk regime), above about 80 percent is high (near-limit regime). Compare the two rows:

1. **Both low**: latency bound. Look at issue-slot utilization (`smsp__issue_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active`; below about 20 percent is severe issue starvation) and at stall reasons.
2. **Memory much higher than compute**: memory bound. Expand the memory breakdown to find which unit, then look at coalescing, sectors per request and bytes per sector.
3. **Compute much higher than memory**: compute bound. Find which pipeline saturates and reduce instructions on it.
4. **Both high**: you are close to the hardware limits of this algorithm. Further gains need a different algorithm, not a better kernel.

blocks.title: Classifying a kernel from two rows

nodes.label:
Speed Of Light:
compute vs memory

scenes.caption: Four branches from two numbers, with the triage guide's thresholds: under about 60 percent is low, over about 80 percent is high.
sgemm_4096: 82 compute, 2 DRAM. Compute bound, and already in the near-limit band.
layernorm_fwd: 5 compute, 78 DRAM. Memory bound at 78 percent of the bus, which is close to what a well written elementwise kernel can reach.
softmax_rows at 33 and bias_add_relu at 13 both land in the both-low branch: latency bound, nothing saturated, and the two largest gaps in the whole profile.

blocks.md: The numbers above are the DRAM constituent, which we can compute by hand. Nsight's Memory Throughput row is the max over L1, L2 and DRAM, so a tiled GEMM that hammers L1 and shared memory can show a high Memory Throughput while its DRAM traffic stays tiny. The triage guide says it directly: a profile showing about 90 percent Memory Throughput can be misleading, so expand the breakdown to see whether DRAM, L2, L1 or the load-store pipeline is the actual limiter.
Speed Of Light does not tell you what to fix. It tells you which of four investigations to open, and whether the kernel has any headroom at all.

blocks.question: A kernel reports Compute (SM) Throughput 88 percent and Memory Throughput 85 percent. What does that combination most likely mean?
options: The measurement is broken, since a kernel cannot be both compute and memory bound
It is close to the hardware limits of this algorithm, so the next gain has to come from doing less work, not from a faster kernel
It is compute bound, because compute is the larger of the two
Occupancy must be 100 percent
blocks.explain: Both rows high is the fourth branch: you are near architectural limits for the current algorithm. The triage guide's stop criteria apply, and it adds a caution: both can be high with inefficient compute and inefficient memory operations both contributing, so confirm that the resource you expected to be busy is the one near peak before declaring victory.

blocks.question: Why does Nsight Compute define Memory Throughput as the maximum over its constituent counters instead of their sum?
options: Because summing could exceed 100 percent and look wrong
Because L1, L2 and DRAM counters are collected in different replay passes and cannot be added
Because a throughput is meant to say how close some unit got to its own peak, and the binding constraint is the unit nearest its own ceiling
Because DRAM always dominates the other memory units
blocks.explain: The metrics guide defines a throughput as how close a portion of the GPU came to peak rate, and says throughput metrics return the maximum percentage of their constituents, chosen to represent the parts of the pipeline that govern peak performance. The slowest relative unit is what limits you, so the max is the meaningful aggregate; the breakdown then names which unit it was.

lessons.title: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it

blocks.md:
A GPU hides latency by switching between resident warps. The Nsight Compute Occupancy section defines **occupancy** as the ratio of the number of active warps per multiprocessor to the maximum number of possible active warps: the percentage of the hardware's ability to process warps that is actually in use.

It also states the rule that people get backwards: higher occupancy does not always result in higher performance, however low occupancy always reduces the ability to hide latencies, resulting in overall performance degradation.

blocks.caption: Resident blocks per SM is a minimum over four independent caps; w is warps per block and r_w is registers per warp. Occupancy is whatever that minimum leaves resident.

blocks.md:
Every term is a hardware limit you can look up. For compute capability 9.0 (H100), from the CUDA compute capability tables and the Hopper tuning guide:

- $W_{\max} = 64$ warps per SM and $T_{\max} = 2048$ threads per SM
- $B_{\text{slots}} = 32$ resident blocks per SM
- $R_{\text{SM}} = 65{,}536$ 32-bit registers per SM (and at most 255 per thread)
- $S_{\text{SM}} = 228$ KB of shared memory per SM

Two allocation rules matter. Registers are allocated to a whole block at once, and register allocations are rounded up per warp (to the nearest 256 registers on compute capability 7.0, per the Best Practices Guide). Shared memory is likewise reserved per resident block. So the arithmetic is quantized, and a kernel can lose a quarter of its occupancy to one extra register.

blocks.code:
R_SM, T_SM, W_SM, B_SLOTS, S_SM = 65536, 2048, 64, 32, 228*1024   # cc 9.0

def occupancy(block, regs, smem_kb=0):
    w  = block // 32
    rw = 256 * -(-regs * 32 // 256)            # registers per warp, rounded up
    caps = [B_SLOTS, T_SM // block, R_SM // (w * rw)]
    if smem_kb: caps.append(S_SM // (smem_kb * 1024))
    blocks = min(caps)
    warps  = min(W_SM, blocks * w)
    return blocks, warps, 100 * warps / W_SM, caps

for cfg in [(256,32,0), (256,40,0), (256,64,0), (256,32,48), (768,32,0)]:
    print(cfg, occupancy(*cfg))

# (256, 32, 0)  -> (8, 64, 100.0, [32, 8, 8])        nothing binds
# (256, 40, 0)  -> (6, 48,  75.0, [32, 8, 6])        registers bind
# (256, 64, 0)  -> (4, 32,  50.0, [32, 8, 4])        registers bind harder
# (256, 32, 48) -> (4, 32,  50.0, [32, 8, 8, 4])     shared memory binds
# (768, 32, 0)  -> (2, 48,  75.0, [32, 2, 2])        block size binds: 2048/768 = 2.67
blocks.caption: Simplified. It reproduces the Best Practices Guide example of 128-thread blocks at 37 registers on compute capability 7.0 (12 blocks, 75 percent) but not the 320-thread case from the same example, where NVIDIA's coarser register allocation granularity gives 4 blocks and 63 percent, not 5 and 78.

scenes.caption: 256 threads per block, 32 registers per thread, no shared memory: 8 blocks fit, 64 warps resident, 100 percent occupancy. Nothing binds.
Add 8 registers per thread. 40 x 32 = 1280 registers per warp, 10,240 per block, so only 6 blocks fit: 48 warps, 75 percent. The register file is the limiter.
At 64 registers per thread a block needs 16,384 registers, so 4 blocks fit: 32 warps, 50 percent. This is what unrolling for more work in flight costs you.
Back to 32 registers but 48 KB of shared memory per block: 228/48 = 4 blocks, so 50 percent. Same occupancy, completely different limiter, and launch__occupancy_limit_shared_mem names it.
768-thread blocks with plenty of registers still cap at 75 percent: 2048 thread slots do not divide by 768, so 512 slots are stranded. Block size is a limiter of its own.

blocks.md:
Nsight Compute does not make you guess which cap bound you. The Occupancy and Launch Statistics sections report the limit from each resource separately: `launch__occupancy_limit_registers`, `launch__occupancy_limit_shared_mem`, `launch__occupancy_limit_warps` (the block-size limit), `launch__occupancy_limit_blocks` and `launch__occupancy_limit_barriers`. The smallest of those is your answer.

The figure below sweeps registers per thread for a fixed block size, which is the shape of curve you should have in your head: occupancy is a staircase, not a slope, and each step is one fewer resident block.

scenes.caption: 256 threads per block. Up to 32 registers per thread you keep 100 percent; the first step down is at 33, and 64 registers costs you half the warps.
128 threads per block: the same staircase, because 4-warp blocks pack the register file just as finely.

768 threads per block: 75 percent at best, because 2048 thread slots fit only two such blocks. Above 40 registers one block needs 36,864 registers and only one fits, so the curve drops to 37.5 percent, and above 80 registers it cannot launch.
1024 threads per block: 100 percent up to 32 registers, then straight to 50, and above 64 registers a block needs more than the whole register file, so the launch cannot be resident at all.

blocks.prompt: A memory-bound kernel sits at 50 percent occupancy because each thread uses 64 registers for an 8-way unrolled load loop. You cut the unrolling to get back to 100 percent occupancy. What happens to the kernel's time?
blocks.reveal:
**It can easily get slower.** Unrolling was what kept many independent loads in flight per warp. Saturating DRAM needs enough bytes in flight, which by Little's law is about achievable bandwidth times memory latency. The triage guide lists two tools for it: more resident warps and more independent loads per warp. You traded one for the other.

The Best Practices Guide makes the same point from the other side: a lower occupancy kernel has more registers per thread, which may mean less spilling to local memory, and with high exposed instruction-level parallelism it is sometimes possible to fully cover latency at low occupancy. Measure the duration, not the occupancy number.

blocks.md:
So when is more occupancy the right move? The triage guide's two-by-two is the cleanest version:

- **Low occupancy, low pipeline utilization**: launch more warps or give each warp more independent work.
- **Low occupancy, high pipeline utilization**: more warps are counter-productive, the busy pipe cannot absorb them. Reduce work on that pipe instead.
- **High occupancy, low pipeline utilization**: warps are present but not issuing. Latency bound; chase stalls and in-flight work, not occupancy.
- **High occupancy, high pipeline utilization**: the SM is saturated. Change the algorithm.

There is also a cheap experiment: raise the dynamic shared memory argument of the launch without using it. Occupancy drops, nothing else changes, and you measure how sensitive the kernel actually is.

One more distinction. **Theoretical occupancy** (`sm__maximum_warps_per_active_cycle_pct`) is the arithmetic above: what the launch configuration allows. **Achieved occupancy** (`sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active`, the metric that CUPTI's old `achieved_occupancy` maps to) is what the hardware actually averaged over the run. A large discrepancy between them typically indicates highly imbalanced workloads: blocks of very different cost, or a tail where most SMs have already finished.

The tail is worth checking first, with `launch__waves_per_multiprocessor`. Our `bias_add_relu` launched as 16,384 blocks of 256 threads with 6 blocks resident per SM on 132 SMs runs 20.7 waves, so its tail costs under 5 percent. A kernel at 0.8 waves per SM has no tail problem to fix; it has a grid problem.

Occupancy is a capability, not an achievement. 100 percent occupancy with 5 percent of peak throughput is a latency-bound kernel with plenty of warps and nothing for them to do, and the fix has nothing to do with occupancy.

Low occupancy always costs you latency hiding; high occupancy does not always buy you speed. Use the `launch__occupancy_limit_*` metrics to learn which resource caps you, then decide whether that cap is actually the thing hurting the kernel.

blocks.question: On an H100, a kernel uses 256-thread blocks, 40 registers per thread and 32 KB of shared memory per block. Which resource limits occupancy?
options: Shared memory: 228/32 allows 7 blocks
Registers: 10,240 registers per block allows 6 blocks, fewer than the 7 that shared memory and the 8 that thread slots allow
Block slots: 32 resident blocks per SM
Nothing: the configuration reaches 100 percent occupancy
blocks.explain: Thread slots allow 2048/256 = 8 blocks; shared memory allows 228/32 = 7; registers need 40 x 32 = 1280 per warp and 8 x 1280 = 10,240 per block, so 65,536/10,240 = 6. The minimum is 6 blocks, 48 warps, 75 percent, and the limiter is the register file. Nsight Compute would show the same split across launch__occupancy_limit_registers, _shared_mem and _warps.

blocks.question: Theoretical occupancy is 75 percent but achieved occupancy is 31 percent. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The launch configuration is wrong and should use smaller blocks
The register allocation granularity was not accounted for
Shared memory is the real limiter rather than registers
The work is unbalanced: blocks differ a lot in cost, or most SMs are idle during a long tail
blocks.explain: Theoretical occupancy is what the launch configuration allows; achieved occupancy is the time average the hardware reached. Nsight Compute's own Occupancy section says large discrepancies between theoretical and achieved occupancy typically indicate highly imbalanced workloads. Check waves per SM and the per-SM active-cycle spread before touching registers or block size.

lessons.title: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return

blocks.md:
A single kernel's Speed Of Light rows tell you whether it has headroom. Across a real application with dozens of kernels and several launch configurations each, you need a number you can sort by. That number is the **SOL gap** converted into time.

Let $L$ be the limiter SOL of a kernel, the larger of its compute and memory throughput expressed as a fraction. If the kernel's limiter ran at 100 percent of peak for the same work, the kernel would take $t \cdot L$ instead of $t$. The difference is the absolute headroom, in milliseconds, which is the only currency that compares kernels of different sizes.

blocks.tex: t_{\mathrm{SOL}} = t \cdot L, \qquad \text{gap} = 1 - L, \qquad \Delta t_{\max} = n \, t \,(1 - L), \qquad \Delta t_{\text{real}} = n \, t \left(1 - \frac{L}{L^{*}}\right)^{+}
blocks.caption: n is launches per iteration. The last form replaces the unreachable 100 percent target with an attainable one, L star, and clamps at zero.

blocks.md:
Why the second form matters: nobody reaches 100 percent of a peak sustained rate. A well written elementwise kernel reaches roughly 80 percent of DRAM peak; a tuned GEMM reaches roughly 90 percent of its pipeline. Choosing an $L^{*}$ per kernel class turns a theoretical gap into an estimate of what a competent rewrite can win, and it changes the ranking.

Here is the whole profile, ranked three different ways.

blocks.code:
wall = 14.52                                  # ms per iteration, from the timeline
# name, launches, ms each, limiter SOL, attainable SOL target
rows = [('sgemm_4096',    2, 2.49889, 0.8209, 0.90),
        ('layernorm_fwd', 2, 0.05162, 0.7761, 0.85),
        ('softmax_rows',  1, 0.18302, 0.3284, 0.80),
        ('bias_add_relu', 2, 0.31957, 0.1254, 0.80)]

for name, n, t, L, star in rows:
    tot = n * t
    print(f'{name:14s} {tot:6.3f} ms {100*tot/wall:5.2f}% of wall  '
          f'SOL {100*L:5.1f}  gap {100*(1-L):5.1f}  '
          f'save@100 {tot*(1-L):6.3f}  save@target {tot*max(0,1-L/star):6.3f}')

# sgemm_4096      4.998 ms 34.42% of wall  SOL  82.1  gap  17.9  save@100  0.895  save@target  0.439
# layernorm_fwd   0.103 ms  0.71% of wall  SOL  77.6  gap  22.4  save@100  0.023  save@target  0.009
# softmax_rows    0.183 ms  1.26% of wall  SOL  32.8  gap  67.2  save@100  0.123  save@target  0.108
# bias_add_relu   0.639 ms  4.40% of wall  SOL  12.5  gap  87.5  save@100  0.559  save@target  0.539
#
# by gap alone : bias_add_relu, softmax_rows, layernorm_fwd, sgemm_4096
# by save@100  : sgemm_4096, bias_add_relu, softmax_rows, layernorm_fwd
# by save@target: bias_add_relu, sgemm_4096, softmax_rows, layernorm_fwd
blocks.caption: Three rankings of the same four kernels. Only the last one is a work plan.

scenes.caption: GPU time per iteration. sgemm_4096 dominates at 4.998 ms of 5.92 ms of kernel time, so the naive plan is to work on it.

Gap alone, drawn as a fraction on the same axis (0.875 is 87.5 percent): it would rank bias_add_relu first and sgemm_4096 last at 0.179. The bars in the other scenes are milliseconds. This ranking ignores how long each kernel runs.
Gap times time: milliseconds recoverable per iteration at a perfect 100 percent limiter. sgemm_4096 leads with 0.895 ms, because 17.9 percent of a big number beats 87.5 percent of a small one.
Now with attainable targets (90 percent for the GEMM pipeline, 80 for DRAM-bound kernels): bias_add_relu moves to first at 0.539 ms and the GEMM falls to 0.439 ms. This is the list you work from.

blocks.prompt: You have one day. From the final ranking, you fix bias_add_relu and win its full 0.539 ms. By how much does the 14.52 ms iteration get faster, and what should you do with the rest of the day?
blocks.reveal:
**By 3.7 percent**, from 14.52 to 13.98 ms. Fixing all four kernels perfectly to target wins 1.095 ms, or 7.5 percent of the iteration.

Meanwhile the timeline from lesson 1 had 8.60 ms of idle plus exposed copies, 59.2 percent of the iteration. Spend the rest of the day there. The SOL gap ranking is the right tool for choosing between kernels, and a terrible tool for deciding whether to work on kernels at all. That is what the timeline pass is for, which is why it comes first.

blocks.md:
Three things the ranking also tells you not to do.

1. **layernorm_fwd has a 22.4 percent gap and is worth 0.009 ms.** A big percentage on a kernel holding 0.71 percent of the wall time is noise. Do not chase it.
2. **softmax_rows has a 67.2 percent gap and is worth 0.108 ms.** The gap is real and diagnosable (a two-pass kernel reading the tensor twice), but at 1.26 percent of the iteration you would be rewriting it for a 0.7 percent win.
3. **sgemm_4096 at 82 percent has the largest absolute gap in theory.** The honest version of that gap is 0.439 ms, and reaching it means matching a tuned library. Substituting cuBLAS is a cheaper way to collect it than writing a better GEMM.

SOL percentages are not the score you optimize. The triage guide is blunt about it: validate every change against absolute kernel duration, because SOL percentages can drop while the kernel gets faster, for example when you reduce the total work. Duration is the ground truth, not SOL percent.

A gap can also be structurally unreachable, and the ranking cannot see that. Common cases:

- **Underfill.** A kernel at less than one wave per SM has a huge gap that no micro-optimization closes; the grid has to change, or the work has to be fused into a neighbor.
- **Irreducible latency chains.** A small reduction's final steps are serial by construction.
- **Traffic you did not count.** A high DRAM throughput with low effective bandwidth is overfetch, not efficiency; the triage guide suggests comparing analytically useful bytes against raw DRAM throughput, and attributing the difference to L2 thrashing and refetches.

And re-rank after every change. Fixing the top kernel usually moves the limiter somewhere else, which is why the triage workflow sends you back to its first decision after each iteration.

Rank by gap times time share, with an attainable target instead of 100 percent. The biggest gap and the biggest win are usually different kernels, and a gap on a kernel with a small time share is never worth a rewrite.

blocks.question: Kernel A: 8.0 ms, limiter SOL 85 percent. Kernel B: 0.6 ms, limiter SOL 10 percent. Which has more absolute headroom at a 100 percent target?
options: Kernel A: 8.0 x 0.15 = 1.20 ms, against kernel B's 0.6 x 0.90 = 0.54 ms
Kernel B, because a 90 percent gap is six times larger than a 15 percent gap
They are equal, since headroom depends only on the gap
Kernel B, because a kernel above 80 percent of peak has no headroom by definition
blocks.explain: Headroom in time is gap times duration: 1.20 ms for A against 0.54 ms for B. The gap percentage alone is the trap. A realistic target changes the margin but not the winner here: at 90 percent for A, 8.0 x (1 - 0.85/0.90) = 0.44 ms, and at 80 percent for B, 0.6 x (1 - 0.10/0.80) = 0.53 ms, which is close enough that you would start with whichever is cheaper to change.

blocks.question: After rewriting a kernel it runs in 0.62 ms instead of 0.90 ms, but its Memory Throughput row fell from 48 percent to 41 percent. What do you conclude?
options: The rewrite is a regression: the kernel now uses the memory system less efficiently
The measurement must be wrong, since less time with the same work implies a higher percent of peak
The rewrite is a 1.45x win; a SOL row can fall when the work itself shrinks, and duration is the thing you validate against
Nothing can be concluded without re-running with cache control disabled
blocks.explain: If the rewrite removed traffic, for example by fusing a pass or improving reuse, the kernel moves fewer bytes in less time, and the percent of peak can fall while the duration improves. The triage guide says to validate every change against absolute kernel duration for exactly this reason. The percentages are for classification, not scoring.

lessons.title: How profiling perturbs what it measures

blocks.md:
Every number so far came out of a tool that changed the machine in order to read it. Nsight Compute, by default, locks the GPU clocks, flushes the caches, serializes kernel launches, and runs your kernel several times. Each of those is a deliberate choice to make metrics reproducible, and each one moves the kernel away from how it behaves inside your application.

Knowing which default is biting you is the difference between a real finding and a week spent optimizing an artifact.

Start with **replay**, because it drives the rest. Not all metrics can be collected in one pass: the hardware can only read a limited number of counters simultaneously, and software-patched counters would distort the hardware ones. So Nsight Compute groups the requested metrics into passes and replays the kernel once per pass.

In the default **kernel replay**, all GPU memory the kernel can access is saved before the first pass, the subset it writes is identified, and that subset is restored before each later pass, so every pass sees the same input. If one pass suffices, no save or restore happens at all.

scenes.caption: Before anything runs, the tool pins the clocks to their boost value so the kernel's position in the application stops mattering.
The application launches the kernel once. The tool intercepts it, saves every byte of GPU memory the kernel can access, and flushes L1 and L2 so the first pass sees cold caches.
Pass one runs the kernel and reads the first group of counters. The kernel really executed, and its writes really landed.
For pass two the written memory is restored and the caches are flushed again, so the kernel sees identical inputs and an identical cache state. Repeat for every pass the metric set needs.
The application sees one launch and one result. It waited for several executions plus the save, restore and flush around each of them.

blocks.md:
The consequences are specific and documented.

- **Clock locking.** Metric values depend on the current SM and memory clocks. A kernel that is first in the application usually runs at lower clocks; one that follows a busy phase runs at higher clocks; and with replay the value could even depend on which pass read it. Nsight Compute therefore limits clocks to their boost value by default. Nsight Systems does not. `--clock-control none` turns it off.
- **Cache state.** The tool can save and restore device memory but not the contents of L1 and L2, so by default it flushes all GPU caches before each pass. Each pass then behaves as if the kernel ran in complete isolation.

If the kernel in your application reads data a predecessor left warm in L2, that default makes it look slower than it really is. The documented remedy is `--cache-control none` together with `--replay-mode application` or range replay, so the application primes the caches itself.

- **Serialization.** Launches are serialized unless you use a dedicated replay mode, because metrics have to be attributable to a specific kernel and because concurrent kernels on one device make values vary widely. If your kernels are meant to run concurrently, that interference disappears from the measurement. **Range replay** captures and replays whole ranges of API calls and kernel launches, so the kernels inside the range run without serialization, with metrics attributed to the range rather than to individual kernels.

blocks.code:
# Question A: what limits THIS kernel, in isolation? (defaults are right)
ncu --set full -k sgemm_4096 -s 2 -c 1 -o report ./app

# Question B: how does this kernel behave inside the real application?
ncu --replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none \
    --section SpeedOfLight --section Occupancy -k sgemm_4096 ./app

# Kernels that must run concurrently for the measurement to mean anything
ncu --replay-mode range --cache-control none ./app

# Iterating: one representative launch, a small section set
ncu --section SpeedOfLight -k regex:"bias_add" -c 1 ./app
blocks.caption: The flags are a statement about which question you are asking. Keep them identical across runs you compare, unless the control itself is the variable.

blocks.md:
Overhead has three sources, and they are not equal. Hardware counters cost very little. Launch and device attributes cost nothing at runtime. Software-patched metrics, which rewrite the kernel's instructions to count things, cost the most, which is why Nsight Compute collects them in separate passes and never measures duration in such a pass.

On top of that, there is a relatively high one-time cost for the first profiled kernel in each CUDA context to build the metric configuration, and that cost does not recur for later kernels in the same context if the metric list is unchanged.

The practical consequence: process wall time can explode while the reported kernel duration does not move at all.

blocks.title: Replay passes multiply execution, not reported duration

scenes.caption: A 0.32 ms kernel profiled with one pass: it executes once. Reported duration 0.32 ms.
Four passes: 1.28 ms of GPU execution, plus a save, three restores and four cache flushes that this bar does not even count. Reported duration: still 0.32 ms.

A full section set can need many more. At twelve passes the kernel has run 3.84 ms worth of work to produce one 0.32 ms number. Simplified: real overhead is higher, since memory restore scales with how much the kernel writes.

blocks.prompt: Nsight Systems reports 0.28 ms for a kernel. Nsight Compute reports 0.33 ms for the same kernel in the same application. Which one is wrong?
blocks.reveal:
**Neither, and the direction is expected.** Nsight Compute inserts a wait-for-idle and a semaphore timestamp after launch setup and before the grid is submitted, so its start timestamp is taken before any block reaches an SM, and another at the end. Nsight Systems times much closer to the first and last instruction, and the documentation states the consequence: Nsight Systems should generally report shorter durations.

Clock locking and cache flushing widen the gap further. The triage guide's rule of thumb: divergence beyond roughly 2x warrants investigation of clock control, cache control or replay-mode effects. 18 percent is not that.

blocks.md: Short kernels are where profiling lies most. Counters for one metric can come from different passes, and if the kernel does not reach a steady state, generally above about 20 microseconds, a derived ratio such as a hit rate can be badly wrong. That is also one of the documented reasons a percent-of-peak metric can read above 100 percent. The fixes: profile a bigger workload, or request fewer metrics per run so related counters land in one pass.

Two smaller hygiene rules worth building into your habits.

- **Warm up, then measure.** Enable persistence mode so the driver stays initialized, and skip the first launches with `-s`/`--launch-skip` so you are not profiling a cold context, a cold allocator and a cold instruction cache.
- **Other engines share the chip.** The display, copy engines and video encoders touch L2, DRAM, PCIe and NVLink. For a short kernel, that traffic shows up in your DRAM numbers and cannot be separated from the SM's own. Profile on a GPU with no active display and no other processes.

And keep capture settings stable across the runs you compare. A before-and-after where one side had cache control on is not a comparison.

Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

blocks.question: A kernel reads a 40 MB table that the previous kernel in the application just wrote, and the GPU has 50 MB of L2. Under default Nsight Compute settings it looks much slower than in the application. Why?
options: Because clock locking lowers the SM clock for memory-bound kernels
Because the tool flushes all GPU caches before each replay pass, so the kernel reads from DRAM instead of the warm L2 it would hit in the application
Because kernel replay restores the table's contents, which invalidates it
Because serialization prevents the two kernels from overlapping
blocks.explain: The tool can save and restore device memory but not cache contents, so by default it flushes caches before each pass to make counters deterministic: each pass behaves as if the kernel ran in complete isolation. For a cache-sensitive measurement that is the wrong question. Use --replay-mode application with --cache-control none and let the application prime the caches itself.

blocks.question: You profile with `--set full` and the application takes 30 times longer, but the reported kernel durations are unchanged. What is the right reading?
options: The durations are stale and should be taken from Nsight Systems instead
The kernels have become slower and the tool is hiding it
Expected: a full metric set needs many replay passes plus save, restore and flush around each, none of which is included in the reported duration
Software-patched metrics have inflated the reported duration
blocks.explain: More metrics means more passes, and the per-pass preparation and post-processing is explicitly not included in the reported duration. The documentation notes the same thing in reverse: because of that overhead you cannot derive a kernel's duration from host timers or CUDA events while profiling with Nsight Compute. Duration is also never collected in a software-patching pass, so those metrics do not distort it.

blocks.question: Which single profiling decision most often invalidates a comparison between two versions of a kernel?
options: Changing the capture configuration between the two runs, for example clock, cache or replay settings
Profiling on a GPU that has a display attached
Using the basic section set instead of the full one
Reporting durations in microseconds rather than milliseconds
blocks.explain: Both the triage guide and the profiling guide insist on it: keep capture settings stable while comparing runs, and keep cache-control and replay settings identical unless the policy itself is the variable under test. A display-attached GPU adds noise and a smaller section set loses detail, but a changed control turns a measurement into an incomparable one.
